Trees, climbing shrubs, or lianas; stipules absent. Leaves compound, odd-pinnate or trifoliate, indumentum of simple trichomes, the blade sometimes with glandular dots on the underside, margin entire; petiole and petiolules pulvinated. Inflorescences in panicles, racemes, or spike-like, axillary or terminal. Flowers bisexual, white, yellowish, or pale pink; sepals 5, valvate or imbricate; petals 5, free; stamens 10, forming a short tube at the base; ovary superior, carpels 1-5, style one per carpel; ovules 2 per carpel. Fruit in follicles, often red; seeds 1 per fruit, black, the aril bright red, yellow, white, or orange.
The family consists of 16 genera and about 300–350 species, pantropical, with a distribution center in western Africa; for tropical America, 5 genera and 108 species are known; 3 genera and 9 species in CR.
It is characterized by its compound leaves, mainly trifoliate or odd-pinnate, leaflets alternate on the rachis, sometimes with dendritic trichomes, petioles clearly pulvinated, stipules absent, and the fruit follicles with a black seed with a reddish basal aril. In vegetative form, its general appearance relates it directly to the family Fabaceae, but several of the characteristics mentioned earlier allow it to be separated.
Traditionally, the family has been placed within the Order Rosales, or in close relation to the Order Sapindales, and some have suggested a link between such Orders. However, recent molecular studies suggest that its placement is in the Order Oxalidales, along with families such as: Oxalidaceae, Cunnoniaceae, Elaeocarpaceae, etc.

Tree, 3.5-11 (13) m tall; trunk usually 6-15 cm dbh; bark with moderately close, deep vertical fissures, but not flaking; young stems, axes of inflorescences, petioles, and underside of veins densely rufous-pubescent, the trichomes pinnately branched, often somewhat stalked. Petioles to 9 cm long; blades broadly elliptic, obtuse to abruptly short-acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, 9-35 cm long, 6-18 cm wide, denticulate, the surface below canescent and completely covered with trichomes, these sessile, stellate, in part with a brown center; veins 5, dark. Panicles large, terminal, 18-22 cm long, branched many times, the branches ± flattened or angulate; flowers ± sessile; hypanthium and calyx together 1.5-2 mm long, campanulate, the teeth obscure or lacking; petals 5, white, obovate, to 1.5 mm long. Berries round to depressedglobose, to 6 mm diam, white to lavender-blue, probably becoming purple-black at full maturity; seeds numerous, minute. Croat 5693, 15070. Known only from shoreline north of the dock and south of Fairchild Point, but undoubtedly more abundant. Seasonal behavior uncertain. Flowers at least in January, February, and May. Mature fruits have been seen in April, May, and October. Easily confused with Miconia argentea, which is similar in most respects except pubescence, trunk bark, and stature. The species ranges from Mexico to Panama and Venezuela; West Indies. In Panama, the species is known only from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Panama and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone.

Androdioecious liana or scandent shrub; young stems, petioles, and axes of inflorescences with moderate to dense stellate pubescence interspersed with simple trichomes. Petioles 3-10 mm long, winged full length; blades elliptic to obovate, rounded to abruptly acuminate (rarely short-acuminate), acute to obtuse and decurrent on petiole at base, 5-18 cm long, 3-8 cm wide, the pubescence minute, pustular, stellate on both surfaces, the simple trichomes mostly restricted to veins; lateral veins in 15-25 pairs. Panicles spikelike; flowers unisexual, usually subsessile, 4-5 mm broad, closely congested; sepals 5; petals (2)3(4), pale yellow to greenish-white, rounded at apex, soon falling, the margin folded inward; stamens numerous, to ca 5 mm long, reduced in pistillate flowers; pistils reduced in staminate flowers; style usually directed to one side; stigma ± spatulate-truncate. Follicle 1, glabrous, shiny, dark brown, 5-7 mm long (excluding prominent beak), dehiscing on one side from style downward to expose seed; seeds 1-4, shiny, black, 3-4 mm long, enveloped at least in part by a deeply lacerate red aril. Frequent along the shore and in the forest. Flowering may be induced throughout much of the year, but the chief flowering period is the early dry season (December to March, especially January and February). Flowering appears to be induced by drought. Severing a vine in the proper stage of bud will soon cause the flowers to open. The fruits mature mostly from March to May (sometimes from February). Mexico to Colombia.

Shrub or small tree, 1-4 m, moderately to densely covered with flexuous, hooked or feathery trichomes, hyaline, and moderately intermixed with tiny, oblong glands, on young twigs, petioles, primary veins raised on the undersides of leaves and [inflorescences]. Leaves 10—29(—39) X (6—)11-21.5 cm, broadly elliptical to elliptical-ovate, broadly rounded and obliquely cordate at the base, shortly acuminate at the apex, inconspicuously wavy-denticulate, glabrous on the adaxial surface, moderately covered on the abaxial surface with a mixture of simple, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes on the secondary and higher order veins, palmately 5-7-nerved. [Inflorescences] with bracteoles 0.5-1 mm, subulate, persistent. [Flowers] with pedicel 1.5-2.5 mm, 5-merous, the hypanthium sparsely covered with a mixture of star-shaped, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes; calyx with lobes 0.25-0.5 mm, wavy and apiculate, the external teeth ca. 0.25 mm, not projecting beyond the lobes, tuberculate; petals white or pale pink, 2.5—4(—5) X 1.5(—3) mm, obovate-oblong, glabrous; anthers yellow, subequal, 1.5-2 mm, oblong, bilocular, with a truncate to retuse pore, the connective without appendage; ovary ca. 3/4 inferior, 5-locular, apex sparsely glandular-pubescent, without a neck; style 3-4 mm, glabrous; stigma not expanded. [Fruits] black purple at maturity, 5-6 X 5-6 mm; seeds 0.5-0.75 mm, broadly deltoid in outline, rounded-angled, smooth, the raphe extended on all sides to form a swollen edge, like a wing. Wet and very wet forest, riverbanks, 50-700 m; Caribbean slope. [The Cordillera de Talamanca], San Carlos Plain, Pacific slope, [the northern part of the Costeña Range (Fila Tinamastes)], [the southern part of the Nicoya Peninsula], [the protected area of P.N. Carara], regions of Puriscal and Golfo Dulce. Fl. Apr., Jul., Aug., Nov., Dec. [Miconia simplex is] recognized by its large leaves, broadly rounded to obliquely cordate at the base and shortly acuminate at the apex, the connective of the anthers without appendage, the ovary 5-locular, and the seeds with an inflated wing-like margin.

Polygamous tree, to 35 m high; trunk ca 1 m dbh, buttressed; outer bark with short fissures, thick, irregular on the inner edge; inner bark reddish with white mottling, forming sap droplets; sap yellow, viscid, with the odor of fresh pumpkin; wood white, soft, lightweight; [the subject plant] glabrous except for dense, minute, ferruginous trichomes on young stems and inflorescences. Petioles 2-4 cm long, stout; blades oblong, rounded to emarginate at apex, mostly obtuse at base, 11-20 cm long, 4.5-9.5 cm wide (to 30 cm long and 8.5 cm wide on juvenile [specific specimens]), coriaceous; lateral veins very fine and parallel, secondary lateral veins lacking. Racemes short, to 4.5 cm long; inflorescence branches, petals, and sepals densely ferruginoustomentose; pedicels less than 5 mm long; buds globose; sepals 4, ± orbicular to broadly elliptic, concave, ca 6-8 mm long, yellow, markedly unequal in width on a single flower, the outermost wider, about half as wide as long.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.

Locating an individual
Intersection of the Southwest Trail (SSO) with the Hartshorn Trail (SHA).
Distribution
From Mexico to Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela, and the Antilles. In Costa Rica, 0-1100 m; Both slopes of the Talamanca Mountain Range; Caribbean slope, Central Mountain Range, Plains of the Guatusos and San Carlos; Pacific slope, Central Pacific, Osa Peninsula.
Habit
Tree, 8-612(-40) m.
Leaves
Leaves 13-39 x 6-22 cm, elliptical to elliptic-ovate, 5-veined.
Flowers
Flowers 5(-6-7)-merous; calyx 0.5-1 mm, inconspicuously lobed, the outer teeth about 0.5 mm, subulate; petals 2-2.5 mm, glabrous.
Fruits
Fruits 0.4-0.5 cm.
Diagnosis
Tree plants; young twigs (and petioles and axes of the inflorescences) densely covered with massively dendritic and shortly pediculate trichomes (sometimes simple and longer on the interpetiolar ridge), the underside of the leaves and hypanthium copiously covered with mostly creamy starry-lepidote trichomes; leaves 5-veined, conspicuously discolorous (green on the adaxial side and light brown on the abaxial side), with petioles deeply longitudinally striated; inflorescences panicles with sessile and glomerulate flowers; flowers 5(-6-7)-merous, with the calyx inconspicuously lobed, with glabrous petals, the stamens with slightly anisomorphic anthers and the ovary 3-locular. It is very similar to
M. argentea
, whose twigs are conspicuously laterally angled (completely quadrangular in
M. elata
) and whose leaves have short and strongly revolute bases, forming a sort of domatia on each side of the adaxial apex of the petiole (flattened in
M. elata
).
Habitat
Wet and very wet forest.
Phenology
Flowers observed in September and November. Fruits observed from March to May, in September and November.

Shrub or small tree, 1-4 m, moderately to densely covered with flexuous, hooked or feathery trichomes, hyaline, and moderately intermixed with tiny, oblong glands, on young twigs, petioles, primary veins raised on the undersides of leaves and inflorescences. Leaves 10—29(—39) X (6—)11-21.5 cm, broadly elliptical to elliptical-ovate, broadly rounded and obliquely cordate at the base, shortly acuminate at the apex, inconspicuously wavy-denticulate, glabrous on the adaxial surface, moderately covered on the abaxial surface with a mixture of simple, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes on the secondary and higher order veins, palmately 5-7-nerved. Inflorescences with bracteoles 0.5-1 mm, subulate, persistent. Flowers with pedicel 1.5-2.5 mm, 5-merous, the hypanthium sparsely covered with a mixture of star-shaped, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes; calyx with lobes 0.25-0.5 mm, wavy and apiculate, the external teeth ca. 0.25 mm, not projecting beyond the lobes, tuberculate; petals white or pale pink, 2.5—4(—5) X 1.5(—3) mm, obovate-oblong, glabrous; anthers yellow, subequal, 1.5-2 mm, oblong, bilocular, with a truncate to retuse pore, the connective without appendage; ovary ca. 3/4 inferior, 5-locular, apex sparsely glandular-pubescent, without a neck; style 3-4 mm, glabrous; stigma not expanded. Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub, Small Tree 
90. Posoqueria Aubl. By C.M. Taylor. Trees, small trees or terrestrial shrubs, unarmed, the flowers bisexual. Opposite leaves, isophyllous, entire, without domatia, the tertiary and higher order veins little visible on the underside or not visible; interpetiolar stipules, lanceolate to elliptical or oblanceolate, caducous, blunt to acute, flattened in bud. Terminal inflorescences, corymbiform, few-flowered to many-flowered, bracteate, upright to deflexed, the cimosal axes. Pedicellate flowers, bisexual, homostylous and apparently protandrous; calyx limb briefly 5-lobed, without calycophylls; corolla hypocratemeric with a slender and elongated tube (generally 2-4 mm in diameter), in bud more or less straight or with all lobes deflexed, white sometimes turning yellow after anthesis, glabrescent to papillose inside and often hirtellous in the throat and on the bases of the lobes, the lobes 5, quincuncial in bud, sometimes unequal in size in one flower, without appendage; anthers 5, exserted on developed and sometimes unequal filaments, dorsifixed near the base, with a triangular and acute apical appendage and a basal appendage of varied shape; stigmas 2, linear, erect and slightly coherent, included, located near or above 1/2 of the corolla tube; ovaries (1)2-locular, the ovules numerous, axillary. Fruits in berries, fleshy to coriaceous, subglobose to ellipsoidal, brown, yellow or orange; seeds subglobose to angular, smooth, with aril cream to orange. 14 spp. Mexico to northern Bolivia, northeastern Argentina, Cuba, Jamaica. In fertile state, Posoqueria is often confused with Alibertia and Randia; both differ by having the convolute aestivation of the corolla and unisexual flowers, and are distinguished from Tocoyena which has convolute aestivation and subsessile anthers. In the sterile condition of Posoqueria, its identification is often avoided. The treatment presented here uses several different characters to separate the species in addition to those used by Steyermark (1967) or Macias (1988), particularly the size and shape of the corolla, the arrangement of the androecium, the fruit characters. Often only one fruit develops in an inflorescence. The floral biology of several species of Posoqueria is unusual, and is described in more detail in Taylor et al. (2011): the anthers are cohesive at anthesis in a central group with unequal and bent filaments under tension until the whole is altered by a pollinator, then the filaments pull the anthers explosively and the pollen is forcefully released. The unequal, flexed filaments of these species generally produce a bent flower in bud, with the corolla lobes deflexed about 10-40° in relation to the tube to accommodate the long filaments. This treatment is based on Taylor et al. (2011) and agrees with Dwyer (1980) and Macias (1988) but not with Steyermark (1967) in treating the name Posoqueria panamensis as a synonym of P. latifolia, with the plants previously included in P. panamensis (i.e., Burger and Taylor (1993) now separated into several species.

(2011): the anthers are cohesive at anthesis in a central group with unequal and bent filaments under tension until the whole is altered by a pollinator, then the filaments pull the anthers explosively and the pollen is forcefully released. The unequal, flexed filaments of these species generally produce a bent flower in bud, with the corolla lobes deflexed about 10-40° in relation to the tube to accommodate the long filaments. This treatment is based on Taylor et al. (2011) and agrees with Dwyer (1980) and Macias (1988) but not with Steyermark (1967) in treating the name Posoqueria panamensis as a synonym of P. latifolia, with the plants previously included in P. panamensis (i.e., Burger and Taylor (1993) now separated into several species.
